results.title: Error of rounded integer division
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ and $N$ be integers with $N > 0$, and let $q$ be the integer nearest to the rational number $a/N$ (halves rounded up). Then $|2(a - qN)| \le N$, that is, $a$ differs from $qN$ by at most $N/2$.

results.title: Norm identity for the remainder

results.title: Convergence of the Laplace transform
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $E$ be a complex normed space, $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ and $s \in \mathbb{C}$. The Laplace transform of $f$ converges at $s$ when the function $t \mapsto e^{-st} f(t)$ is integrable on $(0, \infty)$ with respect to Lebesgue measure.

results.title: The one-sided Laplace transform
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $E$ be a complex normed space, $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ and $s \in \mathbb{C}$. The Laplace transform of $f$ at $s$ is the Bochner integral $\int_{(0, \infty)} e^{-st} f(t)\,dt \in E$.

results.title: Laplace transform with a given value
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $E$ be a complex normed space, $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$, $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and $v \in E$. Then $f$ has Laplace transform $v$ at $s$ when the Laplace transform of $f$ converges at $s$, that is, $t \mapsto e^{-st} f(t)$ is integrable on $(0, \infty)$, and the Bochner integral $\int_{(0, \infty)} e^{-st} f(t)\,dt$ equals $v$; as usual this integral is taken to be $0$ when $E$ is not complete.

results.title: Convergence of the Laplace transform under an exponential bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a complex normed space, $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ almost everywhere strongly measurable on $(0, \infty)$, and $a, C \in \mathbb{R}$ with $C \ge 0$ such that $\|f(t)\| \le C e^{a t}$ for all $t \ge 0$. Then for every $s \in \mathbb{C}$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > a$ the Laplace transform of $f$ converges at $s$, that is, $t \mapsto e^{-st} f(t)$ is integrable on $(0, \infty)$.

results.title: Convergence of the Laplace transform under exponential growth
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a complex normed space, $a \in \mathbb{R}$, and $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ locally integrable on $[0, \infty)$ with $\|f(t)\| = O(e^{a t})$ as $t \to \infty$. Then for every $s \in \mathbb{C}$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > a$ the Laplace transform of $f$ converges at $s$, that is, $t \mapsto e^{-st} f(t)$ is integrable on $(0, \infty)$.

results.title: Holomorphy of the Laplace transform under an exponential bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a complex Banach space, $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ almost everywhere strongly measurable on $(0, \infty)$, and $a, C \in \mathbb{R}$ with $C \ge 0$ such that $\|f(t)\| \le C e^{a t}$ for all $t \ge 0$. Then the Laplace transform $s \mapsto \int_{(0, \infty)} e^{-st} f(t)\,dt$ is complex differentiable at every point of the half-plane $\{s \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} s > a\}$.

results.title: Holomorphy of the Laplace transform under exponential growth
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a complex Banach space, $a \in \mathbb{R}$, and $f : \mathbb{R} \to E$ locally integrable on $[0, \infty)$ with $\|f(t)\| = O(e^{a t})$ as $t \to \infty$. results.title: Prepending a part to a multiset
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $m$ and $k$, the map that sends a multiset $t$ of $k$ natural numbers to the multiset obtained from $t$ by adding one copy of $m$ is injective, so it embeds the multisets of size $k$ into all multisets of natural numbers.

results.title: Partitions with fixed perimeter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The perimeter of a partition is its largest part plus its number of parts minus $1$. For a natural number $n$, the partitions with perimeter $n$ form the finite set of all finite multisets $s$ of positive integers whose largest element plus number of elements (counted with multiplicity) equals $n + 1$.

results.title: Membership in the partitions with fixed perimeter
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and $s$ a finite multiset of natural numbers. Then $s$ is a partition with perimeter $n$ if and only if every element of $s$ is positive and the largest element of $s$ (taken to be $0$ if $s$ is empty) plus the number of elements of $s$, counted with multiplicity, equals $n + 1$.

results.title: The partitions of perimeter three
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There are exactly four partitions with perimeter $3$, that is, four finite multisets of positive integers whose largest element plus number of elements (counted with multiplicity) equals $4$.

results.title: Partitions into d-distinct parts
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $d$ be a natural number. A finite multiset $s$ of natural numbers has $d$-distinct parts when no element occurs in $s$ more than once and any two elements $x < y$ of $s$ satisfy $x + d \le y$.

results.title: Examples of 2-distinct partitions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The partition $5 + 3$ has $2$-distinct parts, and the partition $4 + 3$ does not.

results.title: Fixed perimeter partitions into $d$-distinct parts
results.caption: Definition

Here the perimeter of a partition is its largest part plus its number of parts minus $1$, and a partition has $d$-distinct parts when no part repeats and any two parts differ by at least $d$.

results.title: Partitions into d-distinct parts by largest part and length

results.title: Fixed perimeter partitions into parts in one residue class

results.title: 3-partition instances
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of 3-PARTITION is a pair $(a, B)$ of a finite list $a$ of natural numbers and a natural number $B$, the target sum.

results.title: Well-formed 3-partition instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A 3-partition instance $(a, B)$ is well formed when the length of the list $a$ is a multiple of $3$.

results.title: Feasible 3-partition instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $(a, B)$ be a 3-partition instance with $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{N-1})$, and let $m = \lfloor N/3 \rfloor$. The instance is feasible when there is a map $g : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \{0, \dots, m-1\}$ such that for every $t < m$ exactly three indices $j$ satisfy $g(j) = t$, and the sum of $a_j$ over these indices equals $B$.

results.title: 3-PARTITION as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem 3-PARTITION accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a 3-partition instance $(a, B)$ that is well formed (the length of the list $a$ is a multiple of $3$) and feasible (the entries of $a$ can be split into triples each summing to $B$). Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

results.title: 3-PARTITION is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem 3-PARTITION on bitstrings is in NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

results.title: Bucket sort sorts
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function. For every array of elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$, the array returned by bucket sort is nondecreasing: each entry is at most every entry after it.

results.title: Expected occupancy of a bucket in bucket sort
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}$ be independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. For $i < n$, let $N_i$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with $\lfloor n \omega_j \rfloor = i$. Then $\mathbb{E}[N_i] = 1$.

results.title: Variance of a bucket's occupancy in bucket sort
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}$ be independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. For $i < n$, let $N_i$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with $\lfloor n \omega_j \rfloor = i$. Then $\operatorname{Var}(N_i) = 1 - 1/n$.

results.title: Second moment of a bucket's occupancy in bucket sort
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}$ be independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. For $i < n$, let $N_i$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with $\lfloor n \omega_j \rfloor = i$. Then $\mathbb{E}[N_i^2] = 2 - 1/n$.

results.title: The running time of bucket sort is measurable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n$, the function $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ that maps $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ to the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and to $0$ otherwise, is measurable.

results.title: The running time of bucket sort is integrable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n$, let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ map $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ to the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and to $0$ otherwise. Then $T$ is integrable with respect to the product of $n$ copies of the uniform distribution on $[0, 1)$.

results.title: Lower bound on the expected time of bucket sort
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ have independent coordinates, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. Let $T(\omega)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and $T(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $5n \le \mathbb{E}[T]$.

results.title: Upper bound on the expected time of bucket sort
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ have independent coordinates, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. Let $T(\omega)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and $T(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $\mathbb{E}[T] \le 5n + (n - 1)/2$.

results.title: Bucket sort on the empty input has expected time zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the empty array, the only input of length $n = 0$. Its expectation under the product of zero copies of the uniform distribution on $[0, 1)$ is $0$.

results.title: Expected time of bucket sort on one input
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\omega_0$ be uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$, and let $T(\omega_0)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the one-element array $(\omega_0)$ if $\omega_0 \in [0, 1)$, and $T(\omega_0) = 0$ otherwise. Then $\mathbb{E}[T] = 5$.

results.title: Bucket sort runs in expected linear time
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For each $n$, let $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ have independent coordinates, each uniformly distributed on $[0, 1)$. Let $T_n(\omega)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and $T_n(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $\mathbb{E}[T_n] = \Theta(n)$ as $n \to \infty$.

A constant observation has zero entropy

results.title: Shannon entropy
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Shannon entropy in bits of a probability mass function $p$ on a finite type $\alpha$ is $H(p) = -\sum_{a \in \alpha} p(a) \log_2 p(a)$, where a term with $p(a) = 0$ contributes $0$.

results.title: A point mass has zero entropy
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every outcome $a$ of a finite alphabet, the point mass at $a$ has Shannon entropy $0$.

results.title: A constant observation has zero entropy
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For any probability mass function $p$ on a type $\alpha$ and any point $b$ of a finite alphabet $\beta$, the image of $p$ under the constant map $\alpha \to \beta$ with value $b$ has Shannon entropy $0$.

results.title: Entropy is invariant under relabeling
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a probability mass function $p$ on a finite alphabet $\alpha$ and a bijection $e : \alpha \to \beta$ onto a finite alphabet $\beta$, the image of $p$ under $e$ has the same Shannon entropy as $p$.

results.title: Appending a singleton coordinate preserves entropy
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a probability mass function $p$ on a finite alphabet $\alpha$, the image of $p$ under $a \mapsto (a, 0)$ in $\alpha \times \{0\}$ has the same Shannon entropy as $p$.

results.title: Kullback–Leibler divergence on a finite space
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary:
Let $\mu$ and $
u$ be finite measures on a finite type $\alpha$ in which every singleton is measurable, with $\mu \ll 
u$ and $\mu(\alpha) = 
u(\alpha)$. Then the Kullback–Leibler divergence $\mathrm{KL}(\mu \parallel 
u)$, taken as a real number, equals $\sum_{a \in \alpha} \mu(\{a\}) \log (\mu(\{a\}) / 
u(\{a\}))$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and a term with $\mu(\{a\}) = 0$ is $0$.

results.title: Kullback–Leibler divergence of finite probability laws
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be probability mass functions on a finite type $\alpha$ in which every singleton is measurable, such that $p(a) = 0$ whenever $q(a) = 0$, and let $P$ and $Q$ be the measures they define. Then the Kullback–Leibler divergence $\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q)$, taken as a real number, equals $\sum_{a \in \alpha} p(a) \log (p(a) / q(a))$, where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and a term with $p(a) = 0$ is $0$.

results.title: Surprisal
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The surprisal (information content) in bits of an outcome of probability $q$ is $-\log_2 q$, with value $\infty$ when $q = 0$. Formally $q$ ranges over the extended nonnegative reals $[0, \infty]$: the surprisal of $0$ is $\infty$, the surprisal of $q \in (0, \infty)$ is $\max(0, -\log_2 q)$, and the surprisal of $\infty$ is $0$.

results.title: Cross-entropy
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For probability mass functions $p$ and $q$ on a finite alphabet, the cross-entropy of $q$ relative to $p$ is $H(p, q) = \sum_a p(a) \cdot (-\log_2 q(a))$ in bits, a value in $[0, \infty]$. Here $-\log_2 q(a)$ is the surprisal of $a$ under $q$, which is $\infty$ when $q(a) = 0$, and a term with $p(a) = 0$ contributes $0$. So $H(p, q)$ is $\infty$ exactly when $p$ charges an outcome that $q$ rules out.

results.title: Cross-entropy of a point mass
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an outcome $y$ of a finite alphabet and a probability mass function $q$ on it, the cross-entropy $H(\delta_y, q)$ of $q$ relative to the point mass $\delta_y$ at $y$ equals the surprisal $-\log_2 q(y)$ of $y$ under $q$, which is $\infty$ when $q(y) = 0$.

results.title: Cross-entropy is expected surprisal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For probability mass functions $p$ and $q$ on a finite alphabet, the expected surprisal $\mathbb{E}_{a \sim p}[-\log_2 q(a)]$ (with $-\log_2 0 = \infty$), taken as the integral of a $[0, \infty]$-valued function with respect to the law $p$, equals the cross-entropy $H(p, q)$.

results.title: Cross-entropy is entropy plus divergence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For probability mass functions $p$ and $q$ on a finite alphabet, the cross-entropy $H(p, q)$ in bits equals $H(p) + D(p \parallel q) / \ln 2$, where $H(p)$ is the Shannon entropy of $p$ in bits and $D(p \parallel q)$ is the Kullback–Leibler divergence of $p$ from $q$ with the natural logarithm. The identity holds in $[0, \infty]$ with no support hypothesis: when $p$ charges an outcome that $q$ rules out, both sides…

results.title: Gibbs' inequality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The cross-entropy of any prediction `q` is at least the entropy of the truth `p`.

results.title: Equality in Gibbs' inequality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For probability mass functions $p$ and $q$ on a finite alphabet, the cross-entropy $H(p, q)$ in bits equals the Shannon entropy $H(p)$ in bits if and only if $q = p$. Thus log loss is a strictly proper scoring rule.

results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A codon: three nucleotides, each in `Fin 4` (order `A, C, G, T`).

results.title: Positions at which two codons differ
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The positions at which two codons differ.

results.title: Codons differing at exactly one position
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two codons differ at exactly one position.

results.title: Codon change consisting of transitions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Every differing position is a transition (same parity: `A ↔ G` or `C ↔ T`).

results.title: Symmetry of single-position codon changes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Differing at exactly one position is symmetric.

results.title: Symmetry of transition codon changes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Being a transition change is symmetric.

results.title: Goldman–Yang codon exchangeability
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Goldman–Yang exchangeability between codons `i` and `j`: `0` unless they differ at one position; otherwise `κ` for a transition (`1` for a transversion), times `ω` if the amino acid changes.

results.title: Symmetry of Goldman–Yang exchangeabilities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Goldman–Yang exchangeabilities are symmetric.

results.title: Dependence of Goldman–Yang exchangeabilities on ω
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The nonsynonymous exchangeabilities are linear in `ω`, the synonymous ones do not involve it.

results.title: Goldman–Yang codon rate matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Goldman–Yang rate matrix (Goldman & Yang 1994): the GTR matrix with codon frequencies `π` and exchangeabilities `gyExchange`.

results.title: Stationary rate of synonymous substitutions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The stationary rate of synonymous substitutions per codon, `ρ_S = ∑_{i ≠ j, aa i = aa j} π_i Q_ij`. This is the stationary rate when `∑ i, π i = 1`; for unnormalized weights it is scaled by `(∑ i, π i) ^ 2`.

results.title: Stationary rate of nonsynonymous substitutions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The stationary rate of nonsynonymous substitutions per codon, `ρ_N = ∑_{aa i ≠ aa j} π_i Q_ij`. This is the stationary rate when `∑ i, π i = 1`; for unnormalized weights it is scaled by `(∑ i, π i) ^ 2`.

results.title: Number of synonymous sites per codon
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The number of synonymous sites per codon, counted under `ω = 1`: `S = 3 ρ_S(1) / (ρ_S(1) + ρ_N(1))`.

results.title: Number of nonsynonymous sites per codon
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The number of nonsynonymous sites per codon, counted under `ω = 1`: `N = 3 ρ_N(1) / (ρ_S(1) + ρ_N(1))`.

results.title: Synonymous substitution rate per synonymous site (dS)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The synonymous rate per synonymous site, `dS = ρ_S(ω) / S`.

results.title: Nonsynonymous substitution rate per nonsynonymous site (dN)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The nonsynonymous rate per nonsynonymous site, `dN = ρ_N(ω) / N`.

results.title: Off-diagonal entries of the Goldman–Yang rate matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Off the diagonal the Goldman–Yang rate is `gyExchange i j * π j`.

results.title: Goldman–Yang matrix is a rate matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With nonnegative frequencies, `κ ≥ 0` and `ω ≥ 0`, the Goldman–Yang matrix is a rate matrix.

results.title: The Goldman–Yang chain is reversible
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: It is in detailed balance with its codon frequencies.

results.title: Synonymous rate does not depend on ω
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The synonymous rate does not depend on `ω`: `ρ_S(ω) = ρ_S(1)`.

results.title: Nonsynonymous rate is linear in ω
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The nonsynonymous rate is linear in `ω`: `ρ_N(ω) = ω ρ_N(1)`.

results.title: Synonymous and nonsynonymous sites sum to three
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There are three sites per codon: `S + N = 3` when `ρ_S(1) + ρ_N(1) ≠ 0`.

results.title: `dN / dS = ω`
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `dN / dS = ω` in the Goldman–Yang model with sites counted under `ω = 1` (derived; see the module docstring for the site definition), provided `ρ_S(1) > 0` and `ρ_N(1) > 0`.

results.title: Positivity of the synonymous rate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `ρ_S(1) > 0` if the frequencies are nonnegative, `κ > 0`, and some synonymous single change joins two codons of positive frequency.
